sources.title: Brighton and Hove Museums: Repatriation of artefacts to Botswana, 2026
sources.note: Institutional provenance and diplomatic history, 1895 delegation to maintain protectorate status and oppose company takeover. Avoid erroneous wording in older museum blogs that the protectorate was first created in 1895.

sources.title: Neil Parsons: The Abandonment of Phalatswe, 1901 to 1916 (1998)
sources.note: Original University of Botswana landscape-history workshop paper. Shoshong/Phalatswe/Serowe chronology; drought, rinderpest and political pressures; 1900 traveller’s water-for-grain account. This is a historical paper, not present-day water reporting.

sources.title: Brighton and Hove Museums: Making Botswana, Women’s work
sources.note: Original museum research with Khama III Memorial Museum and local partners. Object numbers R4007/65, /87, /98 and Willoughby photographs around 1895. The 1910 girls-to-boys ratio is presented as wider church-school research, not a census of every Ngwato child.

sources.title: Brighton and Hove Museums: Making Botswana, Woodcarving
sources.note: Collection research: R4007/78, communal cooking spoon collected in the 1890s, almost one metre. Only object-specific passage used; simplified protectorate chronology elsewhere on page not followed.

sources.title: Brighton and Hove Museums: Making Botswana, Leatherwork
sources.note: Collection and collaborative oral-history research: R4007/73 cow-forehead leather sandals; contemporary photographs show mixed leather/woven dress. Avoid generalized ancient population claims elsewhere on page.

sources.title: SOAS Special Collections: Semane Setlhoko Khama, 2020
sources.note: Archive research on teacher, church leader and queen mother, with CWM/LMS photographs. Distinguishes teaching and 1900 marriage from later midwifery/medical advocacy under Tshekedi’s regency after 1925.

sources.title: Paul S. Landau: African Church Authority, 1911 to 1924 (2025)
sources.note: Full open-access scholarly document edition directly read, DOI 10.1515/9783111254036-046, in Africa, pp. 349 to 358. Original Ngwato royal papers at Khama III Memorial Museum. Printed p. 357 source D, letter of 12 February 1923, a re tshwarisane, translated let us work hard hand in hand. Uses published transcript, not a claim to autograph inspection.

sources.title: Botswana DailyNews: Repatriated Bangwato artefacts unveiled, 2026
sources.note: Official government reporting from the unveiling, indexed article text checked; direct fetch failed. Confirms physical return and exhibition at Khama III Memorial Museum, not merely a proposed loan.

sources.title: James Green, Material Values of the Teke Peoples of West Central Africa (1880 to 1920), doctoral thesis, 2017
sources.note: Original research abstract read in university repository; full PDF exceeds web extraction size. Abstract supports ecological diversity, trading intermediaries and colonial transformation. Do not claim the entire thesis was read.

sources.title: Levi P. Morton to Frederick T. Frelinghuysen, 6 December 1882, FRUS 1883, document 122
sources.note: Contemporary diplomatic report and English translations of September and October 1880 instruments. Directly read. Morton reports Stanley’s competing account; neither colonial claimant is treated as neutral.

sources.title: Congo Ministry of Culture and Arts, Domaine royal de Mbé, tentative-list submission, 2008
sources.note: State-authored description on UNESCO platform, not a World Heritage inscription. Description distinguishes the Ngantsibi from the king’s wife and describes former capitals, sacred forests, living rites and genealogies. Broad causal claims about the Berlin Conference are not adopted.

sources.title: Henri Brunschwig, La négociation du traité Makoko, Cahiers d’Études africaines 5(17), 1965, pages 5 to 56
sources.note: Edition of Brazza’s 1880 field notes. Publisher bibliographic record and first page directly read; subsequent original article text verified through fully indexed Scribd mirror https://fr.scribd.com/document/870798380/cea-0008-0055-1965-num-5-17-3024. Food/beer printed page 27, river conditions page 34. Observations are attributed, not universalized.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Raffia cloth, 99-13-47
sources.note: Original museum catalogue fully indexed; direct request failed. Early twentieth-century Teke work, Lower Congo-Kasai region. Label explains weave quality and width as negotiated value; record also identifies funerary use.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Teke ancestor figure, 2019.477.3
sources.note: Directly read original curatorial account. Nineteenth-century figure, bonga, skilled carving, commissions, and Ponel’s mid-1880s account of chiefs’ deliberations. Belief in medicinal power is not a clinical efficacy claim.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Kidumu mask, Earth Matters
sources.note: Full original museum text indexed; direct request failed. Quai Branly 71.1932.89.82, probably early twentieth century, collected 1929. Cartwheeling performance and division above/below; not all Teke communities or every court.

sources.title: Journal officiel de la République française, law of 30 November 1882 and attached Makoko instruments
sources.note: Two-page scan with searchable original French official text directly read. Sample is opening of October 3, 1880 act, page 1. Reproduction of a colonial document, not Teke vernacular or the king’s handwritten words.

sources.title: Noemie Arazi and colleagues, History, archaeology and memory of the Swahili-Arab in the Maniema, Democratic Republic of Congo, 2020
sources.note: Original archaeological project report directly read. Introduction dates Kasongo as commercial capital to 1875 and colonial victory to 1894; fieldwork confirms Old Kasongo/Tongoni and built platforms. Figure 3 identifies remains attributed to Tippu Tip’s house.

sources.title: Benedetta Rossi, An Abolitionist Vicious Circle, Slavery & Abolition 45(4), 2024, pages 870 to 910
sources.note: Original archival study checked through publisher’s indexed full text and PDF excerpts; direct fetch intermittently fails. Pages 876 to 878 discuss captive women and Tippu Tip’s self-serving kinship story; How Networks Mobilized and later collaboration sections establish interlocking Zanzibar/European relations. No uncritical acceptance of his claimed peaceful accession.

sources.title: Congo Arab Heritage in Historical Narratives, CAHN final research report
sources.note: Directly read government-hosted final research report. Printed pages 22 to 26 give objects, house-door reuse, CT wood identification and interviews in 2021/2022. Community centre is a request, not a completed facility.

sources.title: Sidney Langford Hinde, The Fall of the Congo Arabs, 1897, pages 184 to 187
sources.note: Primary account of a participant in colonial conquest, explicitly attributed. Direct full-text fetch failed. Relevant original passages reproduced and checked in Oliver and Atmore, Africa since 1800, page 85, hosted by South African History Archive https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/archive-files3/roland_oliver_anthony_atmore_africa_since_1800book4you.org_.pdf and Bruce Vandervort, Wars of Imperial Conquest in Africa, page 143, institutional PDF https://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/23866/1/110.pdf. No alleged room size adopted because transcriptions conflict.

sources.title: Xavier Luffin, Un autre regard sur l’histoire congolaise: les documents arabes et swahilis dans les archives belges (1880 to 1899), 2020
sources.note: Original critical edition directly read. Printed page 27 describes Kasongo Quran schools and 1904 photograph; MRAC.TOB.15 pages 182 to 183 is Sayf bin Rashid’s original Latin-script Swahili letter, 13 May 1891, with Arabic signature; sample joins the manuscript line break in masha/uri. MRAC.TOB.18 page 186 records 410 cloth lengths owed for rice, 25 January 1892. This Sayf is not identified as Tippu Tip’s son Sefu.

sources.title: AfricaMuseum, Ceci n’est pas le collier de Tippo Tip, 2022
sources.note: Museum’s original provenance investigation fully indexed; direct fetch fails. Establishes Kasongo as Tippu Tip and Sefu’s capital, colonial capture in 1893, abandoned objects and competing attribution. Used for ending, not to certify ownership of purported personal objects.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Decoded polygon lies in central/eastern Botswana. Card covers Bangwato polity, not all Tswana-speaking peoples or the whole modern Botswana state. 1914 is only imported endpoint. 1923 letter and post-1925 Semane medical work explicitly dated as later continuity. No alias association.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Imported 1878 to 1914 polygon spans 13.419 to 16.674 E and 6.283 to 2.888 S. Treat as broad Teke/Mbé kingdom record with explicit regional diversity, not homogeneous sovereignty over all Teke peoples. No claimed founding in 1878 or extinction in 1914. Art examples are dated and may come from communities beyond the precise royal core.

Actual map window 1878 to 1914, broad eastern Congo polygon 22.786 to 29.011 E, 6.531 S to 0.343 N. Card explains commercial/military domain rather than asserting uniform bounded modern sovereignty. Kasongo 1893 conquest and wider 1894 defeat precede imported endpoint. No confident 1860 foundation date adopted. Separate local peoples and postconquest society continue; no alias association.
